details:
**Battle of Jericho**
Joshua's most famous victory and the usual giveaway. Following God's instructions, the Israelites marched around the walled city once a day for six days with seven priests blowing trumpets (shofars) and carrying the Ark of the Covenant; on the seventh day they circled it seven times, gave a great shout, and the walls collapsed.

**Successor of Moses**
Joshua, son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, was Moses's assistant and was appointed to lead the Israelites after Moses died. He led the conquest of Canaan, the Promised Land, and the Book of Joshua tells his story.

**Rahab**
A prostitute (harlot) in Jericho who hid the two spies Joshua sent from Shittim, concealing them under stalks of flax on her roof. In return, she and her family were spared when the city fell; she marked her house by hanging a scarlet cord from her window.

**Sun and moon standing still at Gibeon**
During a battle against an alliance of five Amorite kings attacking the Gibeonites, Joshua asked God to make the sun stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon so that the Israelites could finish the fight in daylight. The book claims there was never a day like it, when God heeded the voice of a man.

**Caleb and the twelve spies**
Moses sent twelve men, one from each tribe, to scout Canaan. Only Joshua and Caleb gave a favorable report urging the Israelites to enter; the people nearly stoned them, and God declared that these two would be the only adults of their generation to enter the Promised Land.

**Achan**
An Israelite who took forbidden plunder from Jericho (a Babylonian garment, silver, and a wedge of gold) that was meant to be devoted to God. His sin caused the Israelites' first defeat at Ai; he was identified by casting lots, and Joshua had him and his family stoned in the Valley of Achor.

**Ai**
A city whose first attack failed because of Achan's theft. In the second attempt, Joshua held out his javelin toward the city and used a feigned retreat to lure the defenders of Ai and Bethel out, while a hidden ambush force entered and burned the city.

**Gibeonites' deception**
The Hivite inhabitants of Gibeon, fearing destruction, disguised themselves as travelers from a distant land with worn-out sandals, patched wineskins, and moldy bread. They tricked Joshua into making a peace treaty, and afterward he made them woodcutters and water carriers for the Israelites.

**Battle of Rephidim against the Amalekites**
Joshua's first appearance (Exodus 17), when Moses had him lead the Israelite fighters against the Amalekites. The Israelites prevailed as long as Moses held up his hands on a nearby hill, so Aaron and Hur supported his arms until sunset.

**Crossing the Jordan and the twelve stones**
When priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant stepped into the Jordan River, its waters stopped flowing so the Israelites could cross on dry ground. Twelve stones, one per tribe, were taken from the riverbed as a memorial at Gilgal, and Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the river where the priests had stood.

**Waters of Merom and Hazor**
Joshua defeated a northern coalition led by Jabin, king of Hazor, at the Waters of Merom, then captured and burned Hazor. This completed his conquests, and the book lists 31 kings that he defeated.

**Circumcision at Gibeath Haaraloth**
After crossing the Jordan, Joshua circumcised the generation of Israelite men born in the wilderness, using flint knives, at a place called the "hill of foreskins." It took place at Gilgal before the campaign against Jericho.

**Five kings in the cave at Makkedah**
After the battle at Gibeon, the five Amorite kings hid in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua had the cave sealed with large stones until the battle was over, then brought the kings out, executed them, and hung their bodies on trees.

**Hoshea and Timnath-serah**
Joshua's original name was Hoshea, which Moses changed to Joshua ("Yahweh is salvation"); the name is the same as "Jesus" in Greek. He received the town of Timnath-serah in Ephraim as his inheritance, oversaw the division of the land among the tribes (including the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan), and was buried there.

**Yusha ibn Nun and Khidr**
In Islamic tradition, Joshua (Yusha) is identified as the young servant who traveled with Moses in the Quran's Surah 18 in search of the wise figure Khidr. They carried a fish that came back to life and slipped into the sea at the meeting place of the two seas, and the servant forgot to tell Moses until later.
